quote: Maryland also reduced hospital spending for commercial beneficiaries, cut ED visits and inpatient admissions across all payer types
correct_fact: RTI: commercial hospital spending grew 6.1% slower (correct). But ED visits did NOT fall for Medicare (payment per visit fell, not the rate); ED rate fell for commercial (-2.6%) and Medicaid. Admissions trended down for all payers but the decline was statistically significant only for Medicare.
source_quote: Medicare expenditure savings for ED visits resulted from a decrease in the payment per ED visit in Maryland relative to the comparison group, not a reduction in the ED visit rate ... the difference from the comparison group was only statistically significant for Medicare beneficiaries
proposed_new_text: Maryland also slowed hospital spending growth for commercial members (6.1%), reduced ED visit rates for commercial and Medicaid patients (though not for Medicare), and cut Medicare admissions
notes: Dual-eligible claim confirmed: 'Outcomes improved for ... beneficiaries dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid relative to other Medicare beneficiaries'. Non-teaching sentence: RTI says teaching and high-DSH hospitals had poorer outcomes on readmissions and follow-up than other hospitals — so the sentence is a loose restatement; but RTI also says overall the model 'did not have an impact on the percentage of discharges with a follow-up visit within 14 days for Medicare beneficiaries' — rephrase as 'Teaching and high-DSH hospitals lagged other hospitals on readmissions and follow-up visits.'

quote: When Maryland reduced avoidable hospital admissions, the reduction was concentrated among healthier patients
correct_fact: RTI's final evaluation found the opposite for Medicare: beneficiaries with multiple chronic conditions and dual eligibles had GREATER reductions in expenditures and utilization; RTI attributes easier ED diversion among commercial/non-dual Medicaid patients to their being healthier. Hospitals reported that changing utilization among complex-needs patients was harder. No source found for 'hospitals actually spent more time treating them'.
source_quote: Beneficiaries with multiple chronic conditions and beneficiaries dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid had greater reductions in expenditures and utilization than their subgroup counterparts. ... changing utilization among patients with complex care needs was more challenging.
proposed_new_text: Maryland hospitals reported that reducing avoidable use was hardest among patients with complex care needs, even though the evaluation found the largest Medicare reductions among dual-eligible and multiple-chronic-condition beneficiaries. The model was not associated with population health improvement.
notes: Next sentence ('The sickest patients continued arriving ... spent more time treating them') should be deleted — UNCONFIRMED. The lesson sentence that follows can stand.

quote: The Milbank Fund's evaluation found mixed results on quality metrics and no improvement in overall population health measures like smoking rates or obesity prevalence
correct_fact: The smoking/obesity finding is from the CMS-commissioned RTI final evaluation (2019), not a Milbank evaluation. RTI: 'The All-Payer Model was not associated with population health improvement'; smoking and obesity trends were unaffected; avoidable-utilization effects 'mixed'.
source_quote: Smoking rates generally declined in both groups at similar rates during the All-Payer Model, suggesting that the model did not have any impact on this behavior. ... Obesity increased at similar rates ... suggesting that the model did not have any impact on obesity.
proposed_new_text: The CMS-commissioned RTI evaluation found mixed results on avoidable utilization and no improvement in population health measures such as smoking rates or obesity prevalence
notes: Milbank 'Uniquely Similar' (2020) is cited in the Sources line but its content was not checked against this sentence; RTI is the primary source.

quote: Medicare hospital savings to date \$1.4B
correct_fact: $1.4B = 2014-2018 All-Payer Model cumulative Medicare hospital savings vs national trend (HSCRC). Not 'to date' — the TCOC Model (2019-) has its own savings figures.
source_quote: (search-result summary of HSCRC April 2019 Biannual Report) cumulative Medicare hospital savings $1.4 billion, 2014-2018, vs. $330 million target
proposed_new_text: Medicare hospital savings 2014--2018 \$1.4B
notes: Fig 6.7 (manuscript has a NO-BREAK SPACE after 'vs.' on this line). Same at line 3289 box -> add '2014--2018'. HSCRC report not opened directly (search result only).
